nodes.label: Gemini Gems live in one div, not one file each
nodes.norm_label: gemini gems live in one div, not one file each
nodes.summary: The takeout holds 180 Gemini Gems plus 10 scheduled briefings, not the two files the directory listing suggested: all 180 entries sit inside a single div of the 1.4 MB gemini_gems_data.html, 842 thousand characters of instructions in total. A tag census over the file returned exactly one div and 51 anchors, so counting files or grepping for titles finds nothing and the real count only appears after parsing the div.

nodes.label: Gems sorted into ten thematic tracks
nodes.norm_label: gems sorted into ten thematic tracks
nodes.summary: The 180 Gems were assigned to ten keyword-routed tracks with real counts: Sains Belajar 43, Desain Visual 38, Konten 20, Produktivitas 20, Mengajar 16, Tesis 14, Asisten AI/Bisnis 13, Riset 12, Video 4, Terjadwal 10. Uncategorised items were mapped by hand and the duplicate mappings verified, so /skills/ became a curriculum table with ten track pages instead of a placeholder list.

nodes.label: Excerpt-only publication protects the prompt IP
nodes.norm_label: excerpt-only publication protects the prompt ip
nodes.summary: The generator was written to publish a summary of each Gem rather than the 842 thousand characters of prompt text, on the stated ground that the full prompts are the paid IP and stay behind the gate. Five prompt-only templates were given honest metadata labels instead of invented descriptions, because a generated description the source does not support is a fabrication in a document that claims to be the source.

nodes.label: Full instructions reverse the excerpt decision
nodes.norm_label: full instructions reverse the excerpt decision
nodes.summary: Asked why the instructions read as cut off, the session dropped the excerpt-only design and chose to render the full instruction text publicly with stronger MDX escaping, rather than building a gated ingest pipeline. The trade-off had been decided in-session the day before and was explicitly retracted, which is recorded later in the recap rather than quietly applied.

nodes.label: MDX brace and angle escaping for imported instructions
nodes.norm_label: mdx brace and angle escaping for imported instructions
nodes.summary: Rendering 842 thousand characters of arbitrary prompt text into a Starlight content collection required md_escape to neutralise <, { and } (written as <, {, }). Escaping only the angle bracket had been enough while excerpts were short; the full text is where JSX-ish and expression characters in the source start breaking the page.

nodes.label: Frontmatter title already renders the H1
nodes.norm_label: frontmatter title already renders the h1
nodes.summary: Starlight renders the frontmatter title as the page H1, and the generator was also emitting an H1 in the body, so every generated page shipped a duplicated title. The user's report that a page title was duplicated was correct and the fix was in the generator template, verified live as exactly one <h1> per page.

nodes.label: Body headings demoted to keep the TOC clean
nodes.norm_label: body headings demoted to keep the toc clean
nodes.summary: The imported instruction text carries its own # and ## headers, which Starlight turned into page headings and fed into the 'On this page' table of contents. The generator now demotes them to ### so the sidebar and TOC describe the page rather than the pasted prompt.

nodes.label: Starlight accent overridden through CSS variables
nodes.norm_label: starlight accent overridden through css variables
nodes.summary: Recolouring the site from Starlight's blue to orange was done by setting the accent CSS custom properties for light and dark and pointing customCss at the stylesheet, rather than overriding component rules. Because links, highlights and buttons all read the variables, one scale change moved every accent at once, and the change was verified by grepping both hex values in the live CSS.

nodes.label: WCAG AA orange pair for dark and light
nodes.norm_label: wcag aa orange pair for dark and light
nodes.summary: The first orange was described as not sharp enough, and the sharpened pair was chosen with contrast measured rather than judged: #ff6a00 in dark mode at 6.18:1 and #c2410c in light mode at 5.18:1, both above the 4.5:1 threshold for normal text. The vividness request and the accessibility constraint were satisfied in one step instead of traded off.

nodes.label: Stale Bun tree installed two Astro versions
nodes.norm_label: stale bun tree installed two astro versions
nodes.summary: Starlight's own link resolved to astro@7.3.5 while the root had astro@7.3.2, a mixed-version tree left by the install state rather than by any declared range. Pinning, config changes and version hypotheses all failed against this; deleting node_modules and bun.lock and reinstalling left a single astro@7.3.2 and the build returned exit 0, so the long satteri failure was an install-tree defect, not a version drift.

nodes.label: Bun skips the satteri WASI package on CPU mismatch
nodes.norm_label: bun skips the satteri wasi package on cpu mismatch
nodes.summary: bun add prints 'Skip installing @bruits/satteri-wasi32-wasi - cpu mismatch' beside the other skipped platform packages, so the WASI binding is absent from node_modules by the package manager's own decision and not because the install failed. Reading the install as incomplete is what sent the session looking for a missing dependency declaration; the package was never going to be installed on this host.

nodes.label: satteri browser entry pulls the WASI package into the client bundle
nodes.norm_label: satteri browser entry pulls the wasi package into the client bundle
nodes.summary: The build failure is a Rolldown resolution error naming satteri/browser.js as the importer of @bruits/satteri-wasm32-wasi, which is a server-side markdown processor. A resolveId tracer eventually showed satteri being resolved out of @astrojs/starlight's user-component processors, so the path into the client graph runs through Starlight's own integration rather than through anything the project configured.

nodes.label: workerd SSR bundle pulls the browser WASM binding
nodes.norm_label: workerd ssr bundle pulls the browser wasm binding
nodes.summary: After the site was switched to SSR the same unresolvable WASI import reappeared in the server bundle, where the bundler reached satteri's browser binding instead of the Node native binding that does resolve at build time. The gating work therefore could not be completed by making the pages SSR, because the workerd runtime could not be shown to run the vendored binding.

nodes.label: Prerendered middleware redirect baked into a static file
nodes.norm_label: prerendered middleware redirect baked into a static file
nodes.summary: Middleware runs during the build for prerendered pages, so its cookie-less redirect result is written into the static HTML and served as a 200 with a meta-refresh instead of a 302. This is why a prerendered Astro site answers with 200 even though the middleware source contains a redirect, and why the same site under server output still returned the baked page.

nodes.label: Public docs funnel with gated app SSR routes
nodes.norm_label: public docs funnel with gated app ssr routes
nodes.summary: The final architecture follows the pattern already proven in Snipset: documentation is a public funnel and only app/* plus api/private/* are gated on SSR. Gating the docs as well was tried first, produced the baked redirect on every page, and then required a satteri WASM binding under workerd that could not be verified, so wasm vendoring was deferred as follow-up debt rather than done quietly.

nodes.label: Fully static Astro build has no server entry
nodes.norm_label: fully static astro build has no server entry
nodes.summary: A build with every page prerendered leaves dist/server empty, so there is no worker entry to upload to Cloudflare even though the adapter is configured. The assets-only deployment path was evaluated first; the fix that produced a deployable bundle was to turn prerender off for the API routes so the server entry exists again.

nodes.label: cf deploy dies scaffolding npm inside a workspace
nodes.norm_label: cf deploy dies scaffolding npm inside a workspace
nodes.summary: cf deploy cannot be used on this project: it warns that no lock file was detected because the app is a workspace member, then tries to scaffold with npm and dies on 'npm error Cannot read properties of null (reading matches)'. The dry run reproduces it every time, so the failure is the deploy path itself rather than a transient state, and it left no way to deploy except the sanctioned wrangler exception.

nodes.label: locals.runtime.env removed by the Cloudflare adapter
nodes.norm_label: locals.runtime.env removed by the cloudflare adapter
nodes.summary: Reading secrets through locals.runtime.env returned 500 on the live login route because the adapter no longer provides that runtime. The fix is a dynamic import of cloudflare:workers with an ambient .d.ts, which reads workerd secrets at request time and falls back to the local .env during dev.

nodes.label: Authorized redirect URI missing because the JSON registers none
nodes.norm_label: authorized redirect uri missing because the json registers none
nodes.summary: The downloaded client_secret JSON contains no redirect URIs at all, only client_id, project_id, auth/token endpoints and the secret, so nothing in the repository can supply the authorized URI. Until it is registered in Google Cloud Console the callback fails with redirect_uri_mismatch, and that single Console step is the only part of the OAuth flow that could not be done from the machine.

nodes.label: Plain-curl 403 is an edge bot challenge, not an app error
nodes.norm_label: plain-curl 403 is an edge bot challenge, not an app error
nodes.summary: A bare curl against the deployed route intermittently answered 403 while the same route was healthy. The worker tail showed zero exceptions and the response went away with a browser user agent, so the 403 was Cloudflare's edge bot challenge in front of the app and not a failure inside it, which is why the first instinct to debug the login route was wrong.

nodes.label: Adapter writes wrangler.json into the static client output
nodes.norm_label: adapter writes wrangler.json into the static client output
nodes.summary: The build drops a wrangler.json into dist/client/ under the base path, and the file carries the full worker configuration including the D1 binding and the route pattern. It was assessed in session and recorded as follow-up debt to exclude rather than fixed there, so the artifact ships in the static output until someone closes the debt.

nodes.label: Plan probe mismatched the idempotent rerun state
nodes.norm_label: plan probe mismatched the idempotent rerun state
nodes.summary: Task T3's verify step asserted a state that is only true on the first run, so the re-run went red on work that was already done. It was written into the error ledger as a plan-authoring defect and the probe was corrected to accept the idempotent state, after which the runner exited 0 and the plan could be closed as Complete.

nodes.label: Edge cache served mixed old and new documents
nodes.norm_label: edge cache served mixed old and new documents
nodes.summary: After the track pages were deployed, some requests returned the previous version and some the new one, so the site looked internally inconsistent. The cause was edge cache holding pre-purge documents, and a cache purge made the responses coherent; the local build was already the same as what was live.

nodes.label: The prompt text is the paid product, so only summaries were published
nodes.norm_label: the prompt text is the paid product, so only summaries were published
nodes.summary: The 842 thousand characters of prompt are stated to be the paid IP and to stay behind the gate, which is why the published pages carry a summary and the full instructions do not appear. The five prompt-only templates were labelled with honest metadata rather than invented descriptions because the same rule applies to generated text.

nodes.label: The user's request overturned the self-decided excerpt trade-off
nodes.norm_label: the user's request overturned the self-decided excerpt trade-off
nodes.summary: The excerpt-only trade-off had been decided in-session for IP reasons without being asked for, and the recap admits that as the error: because full instructions were requested, full instructions are what went live.

nodes.label: The WASI runtime could not be verified, so full-doc gating was deferred
nodes.norm_label: the wasi runtime could not be verified, so full-doc gating was deferred
nodes.summary: Gating the documentation as well as the app was abandoned because it needs the satteri WASM binding vendored into workerd, and that runtime could not be shown to work. The public-docs funnel was chosen over a gating scheme whose runtime was unproven, and the gap was left as a named follow-up rather than papered over.

nodes.label: Prerendered pages are static assets and never run middleware
nodes.norm_label: prerendered pages are static assets and never run middleware
nodes.summary: Static asset serving bypasses middleware, so a prerendered page cannot be gated at request time no matter what the middleware source says. That is why the gate had to be enforced by SSR enforcement on the app routes instead of by a redirect in the middleware.

nodes.label: Dynamic cloudflare:workers import so node dev still runs
nodes.norm_label: dynamic cloudflare:workers import so node dev still runs
nodes.summary: A static import of cloudflare:workers would break the node dev server and the build, so the module is imported dynamically and the ambient declaration added by hand. The route reads workerd secrets first, then build-time env, so one code path serves both runtimes.

nodes.label: No CI and a broken cf deploy left one approved local wrangler run
nodes.norm_label: no ci and a broken cf deploy left one approved local wrangler run
nodes.summary: CI was rejected by the user and cf deploy crashes on this workspace, so the single deploy ran through a local wrangler deploy under explicit approval. The exception is recorded rather than treated as precedent: the cf-only rule still applies from that point on.

nodes.label: Worker tail and a browser user agent proved the edge was 403ing
nodes.norm_label: worker tail and a browser user agent proved the edge was 403ing
nodes.summary: The worker tail recorded zero exceptions and the 403 disappeared with a browser user agent, so the rejection happened at Cloudflare's edge before the application ran. That evidence is what moved the diagnosis away from the login route.
